questions.article: Nairobi and Peshawar Attacks Completely Anti-Islamic
questions.q: Whom does the editorial hold most responsible for attacks such as those in Peshawar and Nairobi?
options: The foreign media
Not quite. The article says: The leaders who gave Islam a political interpretation.
The leaders who gave Islam a political interpretation
Yes. He calls political Islam “the greatest evil in the present age.”
The victims’ own communities
Not quite. The article says: The leaders who gave Islam a political interpretation.
The governments of the countries attacked
Not quite. The article says: The leaders who gave Islam a political interpretation.
questions.rationale: “The real blame goes less to the attackers themselves than to their intellectual mentors. The real culprits are those leaders who have given a political interpretation to Islam.”

questions.article: Nairobi and Peshawar Attacks Completely Anti-Islamic
questions.q: Some quote the verse “do not take the Jews and the Christians for friends” (5:51) to justify hatred. How does the editorial explain the verse?
options: It was a temporary instruction about those then at war with the Prophet, not a rule about all Jews and Christians
Correct. It gives no ground for hostility today.
It refers only to trade
Not quite. The article says: It was a temporary instruction about those then at war with the Prophet, not a rule about all Jews and Christians.
It was later removed from the Quran
Not quite. The article says: It was a temporary instruction about those then at war with the Prophet, not a rule about all Jews and Christians.
It applies to all non-Muslims for all time
Not quite. The article says: It was a temporary instruction about those then at war with the Prophet, not a rule about all Jews and Christians.
questions.rationale: “The Quranic verse quoted above is neither about all the Jews or Christians, nor is it a permanent teaching. It is a temporary instruction.”

questions.q: Philosopher-kings, collective ownership and home rule were each expected to end oppression. What does the article say they all lacked?
options: The fear of God, which alone keeps those in power to truth and justice
Exactly. Changing systems only changed the hands that held power.
The support of other nations
Not quite. The article says: The fear of God, which alone keeps those in power to truth and justice.
Enough time to prove themselves
Not quite. The article says: The fear of God, which alone keeps those in power to truth and justice.
Trained administrators
Not quite. The article says: The fear of God, which alone keeps those in power to truth and justice.
questions.rationale: “The only factor that can affect true reform is the fear of God. Nothing else can hold a man in power to the observance of proper standards of truth and justice.”

questions.q: Imam Hasan had an army of 60,000, yet gave up the Caliphate after six months. What did his stepping back achieve?
options: It ended civil war, so that Muslim energies turned to constructive work
Yes. “Sometimes stepping back is the way to move forward.”
It gave his family the Caliphate later
Not quite. The article says: It ended civil war, so that Muslim energies turned to constructive work.
It forced his rival to share power
Not quite. The article says: It ended civil war, so that Muslim energies turned to constructive work.
It made Kufa the capital of the empire
Not quite. The article says: It ended civil war, so that Muslim energies turned to constructive work.
questions.rationale: “With Imam Hasan’s stepping back, internecine fighting among Muslims was replaced by internal solidarity.” The article calls it wise pragmatism, not cowardice.

questions.q: The angels feared man would shed blood on earth. Why, in the article’s explanation, did God still create him?
options: The angels’ fear was mistaken
Not quite. The article says: Among mankind would be those who freely choose to submit to God – few, but as precious as grain amid straw.
The earth needed someone to cultivate it
Not quite. The article says: Among mankind would be those who freely choose to submit to God – few, but as precious as grain amid straw.
Among mankind would be those who freely choose to submit to God – few, but as precious as grain amid straw
Well read. Their worth justifies the whole field.
Man would be given no freedom to do wrong
Not quite. The article says: Among mankind would be those who freely choose to submit to God – few, but as precious as grain amid straw.
questions.rationale: “They would be comparatively few in number, but they would be as precious as the grains of a crop. Grain is far outweighed by hay and straw, but so great is its value…”

questions.q: Returning from the Tabuk campaign, the Prophet spoke of going “from lesser jihad to greater jihad.” What is the greater jihad?
options: The journey of pilgrimage
Not quite. The article says: The struggle against one’s own evil desires.
The duty of ruling a state
Not quite. The article says: The struggle against one’s own evil desires.
A larger military campaign
Not quite. The article says: The struggle against one’s own evil desires.
The struggle against one’s own evil desires
Right. It continues every day of a believer’s life.
questions.rationale: “The ‘lesser jihad’ is a military struggle, while the ‘greater jihad’ is the struggle against one’s own evil desires.”

questions.article: War as an Instrument to Acquire Power
questions.q: Why does the article say it is no longer necessary to struggle for political power?
options: Religion forbids all interest in public life
Not quite. The article says: Influence has shifted from politics to institutions, which are open to everyone.
Influence has shifted from politics to institutions, which are open to everyone
Yes. Education, media, research and industry now do what power once did.
Political power has been abolished
Not quite. The article says: Influence has shifted from politics to institutions, which are open to everyone.
Rulers today always act justly
Not quite. The article says: Influence has shifted from politics to institutions, which are open to everyone.
questions.rationale: “The shift of the focus of influence from politics to institutions has rendered political power into nothing but a political headache.”

questions.q: National government, a non-violent political movement, and legislation each failed to produce a good society in India. What, says the article, was the shared mistake?
options: Spending too little money
Not quite. The article says: Thinking in terms of systems instead of reforming individuals.
Thinking in terms of systems instead of reforming individuals
Exactly. The individual is the building block of society.
Copying foreign models
Not quite. The article says: Thinking in terms of systems instead of reforming individuals.
Acting too slowly
Not quite. The article says: Thinking in terms of systems instead of reforming individuals.
questions.rationale: “Our basic shortcoming is to think purely in terms of systems… If individuals are reformed, society follows suit.”

questions.q: What is the author’s “scientific” understanding of peace?
options: Peace exists only where full justice has been done
Not quite. The article says: Peace is the absence of war; justice is a separate goal to be worked for afterwards.
Peace is the absence of war; justice is a separate goal to be worked for afterwards
Correct. Insisting on both together loses both.
Peace is a balance of military strength
Not quite. The article says: Peace is the absence of war; justice is a separate goal to be worked for afterwards.
Peace means the victory of the rightful side
Not quite. The article says: Peace is the absence of war; justice is a separate goal to be worked for afterwards.
questions.rationale: “The purpose of peace is only to normalise the situation so that one may uninterruptedly avail of the opportunities that are present.” Hudaibiya and post-war Japan are given as examples.

questions.q: Every person, says the article, needs something to look up to. How does the believer differ from others in meeting this need?
options: He gives up the need altogether
Not quite. The article says: He passes beyond created things, however grand, to the Creator Himself.
He relies on himself alone
Not quite. The article says: He passes beyond created things, however grand, to the Creator Himself.
He passes beyond created things, however grand, to the Creator Himself
Yes. He is not overawed by wealth or great men.
He looks up only to the wisest of people
Not quite. The article says: He passes beyond created things, however grand, to the Creator Himself.
questions.rationale: “To believe in God is to look up to Him alone, while disbelief is to live in veneration of others besides Him… He presses on until, passing by all creation, he reaches the Creator himself.”
